notes.b: Protein comes from both animal and plant foods, so everyone can meet their needs whatever they eat. Exam answers earn marks for naming a variety of foods from each group.
points: Animal protein sources are meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, cheese and yoghurt. Cheese and yoghurt belong in the list because they are made from milk.
Plant protein sources are soya beans and soya products, pulses (lentils, peas and beans), cereals (wheat, rice, maize and oats), nuts and seeds.
Cereals such as wheat, rice and maize supply protein as well as carbohydrate, so everyday foods like wheat, bread and pasta are plant protein sources.
Potatoes and vegetables contain only small amounts of protein, so they are not counted as main protein sources.
notes.tip: When asked for dietary sources, name three or four different foods from each of animal and plant, for example meat, fish, eggs, milk or cheese, then soya, pulses, cereals and nuts. Marks go for variety, not for repeating one food.

notes.b: Albumin is the protein most people meet first, in the white of an egg. It is a good example of a protein that is tied to one particular food.
points: Albumin is the main protein of egg white (ovalbumin), and it is also found in lean meat.
Lactalbumin, a related albumin, is found in the whey of milk, the watery part left when the casein is removed.
Albumin is a soluble globular protein. It dissolves in water and coagulates (sets) when heated, which is why raw egg white turns solid and white on cooking.
notes.tip: Egg white is albumin, but the yolk is not, so say egg white rather than the whole egg.

notes.b: Casein is the main protein of milk, so it follows milk into every food made from milk. Cheese-making depends on changing it.
points: Casein (the older term is caseinogen) is the main protein of milk.
Casein is present in cheese and yoghurt, the products made from milk.
Casein is coagulated by the enzyme rennin, which is the first step in making cheese because it forms the curd. Acid also coagulates it, which is why milk curdles when it sours.
notes.tip: It is casein, not albumin, that rennin coagulates. Remember that casein is the milk protein and lactalbumin is the whey protein that is left.

notes.b: Gelatine is the protein behind jelly, but it is not found in raw meat. It is made when another protein, collagen, is heated.
points: Gelatine is not present in raw meat; it forms when collagen from animal bones, skin and connective tissue is heated in moisture.
Gelatine sets to a gel when it cools, so it is used in jelly, aspic, gelatine-set mousses and desserts, marshmallows and some sweets.
Gelatine comes from animal sources, so foods set with it are not vegetarian.
notes.tip: Gelatine is made from collagen by heating in moisture. Do not name gelatine as a protein in raw meat, bone or fish flesh; give collagen, myosin, actin or elastin instead.

notes.b: Gluten is the protein that gives wheat bread its structure. It does not exist in dry flour; it is formed when the flour is wet.
points: Gluten is the protein of wheat and wheat flour.
Gluten forms when the proteins gliadin and glutenin, both already present in the flour, are mixed with water. Flour itself contains gliadin and glutenin, not formed gluten.
Gluten is elastic and stretchy, and kneading develops it. It gives bread dough its elastic, stretchy texture and traps the carbon dioxide made by yeast, so the dough rises.
Foods that depend on wheat gluten include bread, pasta, cakes, pastry and other flour products.
notes.tip: If asked what forms gluten, say gliadin and glutenin mixed with water. For a food source of gluten, name wheat or flour.

notes.h: Summary of the proteins and their food sources
notes.b: Each of these proteins is tied to a food or food group. Pairing every named protein with one food is the quickest way to answer a naming question.
points: Albumin: found in egg white and meat, and it sets when heated.
Casein: found in milk, cheese and yoghurt, and it is coagulated by rennin.
Gelatine: found in set desserts such as jelly, and it is made from collagen.
Gluten: found in wheat flour and bread, and it traps gas in dough.
notes.tip: Remember: egg white is albumin, milk is casein, wheat is gluten. Give one correct food for each protein named.

notes.h: Myosin, actin and collagen (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Meat and fish are made of muscle and connective tissue, and each contains its own proteins. Higher Level questions ask you to name them.
points: Myosin and actin are the contractile proteins of muscle, which means they contract to move the muscle. They are found in the flesh of meat and fish.
Collagen is the main protein of connective tissue and is found in meat, fish and bones.
Collagen in meat and fish is the source of gelatine when it is heated in moisture; this is why cheap tough cuts of meat tenderise on slow, moist cooking.
Elastin in meat and globulin in egg are also acceptable answers when asked for proteins in meat or egg.
notes.tip: Higher Level questions ask for one food for each protein named: casein from cheese or milk, actin, myosin and collagen from meat or fish, albumin from eggs, gluten from wheat or flour. For fish, the protein can be myosin, collagen or actin.

keyTerms.definition: A soluble globular protein found in egg white, meat and milk whey.
The main protein of milk, which coagulates when rennin acts on it in cheese-making.
A derived protein that forms when collagen is heated in moisture and sets to a gel on cooling.
A protein formed by chemical or enzymatic action on another protein, such as gelatine from collagen.
The elastic protein network formed when the wheat proteins gliadin and glutenin are mixed with water.
The fibrous protein of connective tissue, which converts to gelatine when heated in moisture.
A fibrous muscle protein that, with actin, forms the contractile filaments of meat and fish.
A muscle protein that, with myosin, forms the contractile filaments of meat and fish.

questions.prompt: Identify a food that supplies each of these proteins: albumin, casein and gluten. Name one animal and one plant protein source in the diet.
questions.model: Albumin: egg white (also meat). Casein: milk, cheese or yoghurt. Gluten: wheat or wheat flour. Animal protein source: for example meat, fish, eggs or milk. Plant protein source: for example soya beans, pulses, cereals, nuts or seeds.

questions.prompt: Explain how gelatine is formed from collagen and describe the foods that contain it. Outline how gluten is formed in bread dough and state why it matters to the texture of bread.
questions.model: Gelatine: a derived protein formed when collagen from animal bones, skin and connective tissue is heated in moisture; it is not present in raw meat; it is used in jelly, aspic and gelatine-set mousses and desserts. Gluten: formed when the wheat proteins gliadin and glutenin are mixed with water; kneading develops an elastic network; the network traps the carbon dioxide made by yeast, so the bread rises and has an open, elastic texture.
